newsitem.title: USA: CBOT must adapt to changing economy, EMU - Arbor.
newsitem.headline: CBOT must adapt to changing economy, EMU - Arbor.

text.p: - U.S. futures and options exchanges must adapt to challenges posed by the enormous changes in the industry and the world economies, Patrick Arbor, the chairman of the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) said at a luncheon on Monday.

Speaking to journalists, Arbor discussed several changes already underway at the CBOT, including a plan to combine certain operations at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) and the CBOT, a proposed trading link between the CBOT and the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE,) and a new electronic system that will allow the exchange to broker cash government securities.
Regarding the latter, Arbor said the unit -- to be known as the Chicago Board Brokerage (CBB) system -- should be launched by the second quarter of 1997, probably by April.
Asked about ongoing progress to combine some operations between the CME and CBOT, Arbor said: "The negotiations are going well, very well."
However, he said it's unlikely that the two exchanges would ever share a common trading facility because each has too great an investment in its own property.
"I can't see the day. Perhaps my successors... will, but it will be down the line.
Arbor also discussed a conversation he had with the U.K.'s Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke over the impact of European Monetary Union.
Arbor said he asked Clarke whether a homogenization of European currencies, and to a lesser extent interest rates, would result in heavy job losses among traders and analysts.
"And the response was: 'It may.' And that's very good for a central banker but it's not very good for an exchange," Arbor said.
Arbor said he believes a link with LIFFE is particularly desirable in light of EMU.
Officials at both LIFFE and the CBOT expect their joint linkage to be in place by May of 1997.
Arbor also said the CBOT must continue to work to reduce government regulation, so as to better compete with over-the-counter trade.
"Federal regulation is choking our business," he said.
